chapter_theme: The first half of the herdswomen's kuravai: on the morning after Kovalan's killing, Madari finds the milk, butter and cattle showing signs of a coming sorrow, and to avert it sets seven herd girls, each pledged by the bull-catch formula to a bull's tamer and named for one of the seven notes, to dance before Kannaki the kuravai of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai; the first song asks that the herders' god come among the cows today.

cast.role: the old herdswoman of Madurai in whose house Kannaki was lodged (named here இடைமுதுமகள்)
the seven herd girls of Madari's kuravai, named for the seven notes and cast as Mayavan, his elder brother, Pinnai and the rest

silappathikaram:17:1-10.reading: Because the morning drum will sound in the palace of the Pandya, whose fish is inscribed on the brow of the Himalaya beside the tiger and the bow and whose orders the kings of Navalam obey, the old herdswoman, saying that today is their turn to bring ghee, calls her daughter Aiyai and comes out with churning rope and churn.
silappathikaram:17:1-10.nuance: The kaathai opens on the Pandya's glory and the ordinary round of service his house draws from the herders (நெய்ம்முறை, their turn to supply ghee) on the morning after his men have killed Kovalan; the king is praised by his emblem and not named. Unlike the Kalittokai's boast that the fish replaced the tiger and the bow, the fish here stands beside them (அயலெழுதிய).
silappathikaram:17:1-10.event: Madari, saying it is their turn to supply ghee to the palace, calls her daughter Aiyai and comes with churning rope and churn.

silappathikaram:17:11-12.reading: The first sign: the milk in the pots will not set, and tears run from the eyes of the bull with the heaped hump; something is coming.
silappathikaram:17:11-12.nuance: Each of the three couplets ends on the same refrain (வருவதொன் றுண்டு), and the prose that follows (lines 17 to 20) gathers them as the old woman's own reading, so the voice is hers though no line names her.
silappathikaram:17:11-12.event: The milk in the pots fails to curdle and the bull sheds tears.

silappathikaram:17:13-14.reading: The second sign: the fragrant butter in the hanging pot does not melt, and the lambs do not leap and play; something is coming.
silappathikaram:17:13-14.nuance: Line 13 reads உருகா உருகும், which taken literally sets 'does not melt' against 'melts'; the prose restatement at lines 18 and 19 has only உருகாமையும் (its not melting), and this reading follows it.
silappathikaram:17:13-14.event: The butter will not melt and the lambs lie still.

silappathikaram:17:15-16.reading: The third sign: the cows stand trembling and lowing in pity, and the bells of the cattle fall; something is coming.
silappathikaram:17:15-16.event: The cows tremble and low, and the cattle's bells drop to the ground.

silappathikaram:17:17-26.reading: Summing up the signs as a sorrow to come, the old woman tells her daughter not to be troubled: with Kannaki, the ornament of the women of the earth, looking on, they will dance the kuravai that Mayavan danced with his elder brother and with long-eyed Pinnai among the boyhood plays of the cattle-yard of Ayarpadi, so that the distress of the cows and calves may pass.
silappathikaram:17:17-26.nuance: The remedy is a rite: a re-enactment of Krishna's childhood dance among the herds, set against an evil the signs do not name. The reader knows what the herders do not, that Kovalan was killed the day before (16:194-217), so the distress of cows and calves the dance is meant to lift stands for a loss already done. Kannaki is placed as the dance's onlooker, not a dancer.
silappathikaram:17:17-26.event: Madari reads the omens as a coming sorrow and resolves to dance the kuravai of Mayavan before Kannaki to avert it.

claims.claim: dancing the kuravai that Mayavan danced among the herds will drive away the distress the omens foretell

silappathikaram:17:27-28.reading: This girl, garlanded with honeyed flowers, will love the man who, unafraid of the black bull's fury, leapt upon it.
silappathikaram:17:27-28.nuance: The pledge is the bull-catch formula of the herders (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான், as in Kalittokai 104), but here no bull is penned and no man leaps: the old woman names each girl by the bull her tamer would take, as the first of the dance's roles. The speaker is inferred from lines 41 to 44, where she sets the seven girls in order.

silappathikaram:17:29-30.reading: The shoulders of this girl with golden bangles belong to the man who subdues the red bull with the mark on its brow.

silappathikaram:17:31-32.reading: This girl with mullai flowers in her hair belongs to the man who rides the strong young bull.
silappathikaram:17:31-32.nuance: This couplet and lines 37 to 38 both pledge a girl to the rider of a young bull (மழவிடை யூர்ந்தாற்கு), told apart only by the epithets மல்லல் and வென்றி.

silappathikaram:17:33-34.reading: The shoulders of this creeper-like girl go only to the man who subdues the white bull with fine spots.

silappathikaram:17:35-36.reading: This good, creeper-like girl with soft breasts goes only to the men who subdue the white bull with golden spots.
silappathikaram:17:35-36.nuance: Nearly the same couplet as lines 33 to 34, with பொற்பொறி for நுண்பொறி and the plural அடர்த்தார்க்கே for the singular.

silappathikaram:17:37-38.reading: This girl with konrai flowers in her hair belongs to the man who rides the victorious young bull.

silappathikaram:17:39-40.reading: This girl like a fresh poovai flower belongs to the man who subdues the pure white bull.
silappathikaram:17:39-40.nuance: With the black bull of line 27, this makes seven bulls for seven girls.

silappathikaram:17:41-50.reading: So, saying to her daughter that these are the seven young girls for whom bulls were raised in the pen, the old herdswoman sets them in the ancient order and names them, going round from the west, after the seven notes: kural, tuttam, kaikkilai, uzhai, ili, vilari and taram, the names the flower-haired one wanted.
silappathikaram:17:41-50.nuance: The ring of dancers is laid out as the circle of the seven notes, so the dance is also a scale. Whose wish the closing words name (விரிதரு பூங்குழல்) is not clear: the old woman, her daughter, or each girl.
silappathikaram:17:41-50.event: Madari sets the seven herd girls in a ring and names them after the seven notes.

silappathikaram:17:51-54.reading: She called kural Mayavan, ili the victorious Vellai (his elder brother), and tuttam the herd girl Pinnai, and said the rest keep their former names in order.
silappathikaram:17:51-54.event: Madari gives three of the notes the roles of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai.

silappathikaram:17:55-58.reading: She sets the places: Pinnai and taram stand in Mayavan's measure, uzhai and vilari in white Vellai's, kaikkilai stands at Pinnai's left, and vilari to the right.
silappathikaram:17:55-58.nuance: The places seem to follow the concords between the notes, so who stands beside whom is a matter of the scale. Line 58 (முத்தைக்கு நல்விளரி தான்) is obscure, and vilari is named in both lines 56 and 58.
silappathikaram:17:55-58.event: Madari assigns each dancer her place in the ring.

silappathikaram:17:59-64.reading: Of them, the one who lays the cool tulasi garland on Mayavan enters the ceaseless kuravai, and the herd girl cries out in wonder that this bangled one is their own Pinnai, set beside the Tiru on the chest of him who measured the world.
silappathikaram:17:59-64.nuance: The sense of திருநோக்கா (line 62) is unsure: whether Pinnai is one Tiru looks upon, or one who does not look to Tiru, the herd girl ranks the herders' own Pinnai with the goddess on Vishnu's chest. Which herd girl cries out (ஆயர் மகள், line 64) is not clear.
silappathikaram:17:59-64.event: The girl playing Pinnai garlands the girl playing Mayavan with tulasi and joins the dance.

silappathikaram:17:65-75.reading: Standing in a true circle with their hands joined in the crab clasp, they work out the dance measures; the first, kural, looks to her kin and says they will sing the sweet mullai tune of the one who broke the kurundu tree in the field, and as she takes kural low, ili level, tuttam strong and vilari low in their due order, her companion takes up the song after her.
silappathikaram:17:65-75.nuance: The kurundu tree recalls a feat of Krishna's boyhood, so the tune chosen is itself a story of the god among the herds.
silappathikaram:17:65-75.event: The seven girls join hands in the ring and begin the mullai song.

silappathikaram:17:76-78.reading: The first song: if Mayavan, who knocked down the fruit using a calf as his throwing stick, comes among our cows today, shall we not hear from his lips the sweet konrai flute, friend?
silappathikaram:17:76-78.nuance: The wish that the herders' god come among the cows today (இன்று) is the rite's answer to the omens, but the herdsmen's guest, whom the household likened to the gem-coloured god (16:48-61), is already dead. The konrai flute is the herders' flute of konrai pods.

links.note: The Kalittokai's herders open their bull-catch by praising the Pandya who removed the tiger and the bow and set his fish in their place; the epic's herders open their kuravai on the Pandya whose fish is inscribed on the Himalaya beside the tiger and the bow.
links.teaches: The same herders' praise of the Pandya emblem is kept in the epic but with the boast of conquest removed, so a work that follows all three kingdoms keeps the mullai custom of beginning with the king while setting the three emblems side by side.

gains.a: the opening's praise of the king gains a precedent: Sangam herders already began the bull-catch songs with the Pandya and his fish
gains.b: the poem's claim that the fish displaced the tiger and the bow gains a later telling that does not keep it, so the claim reads as praise rather than settled history

links.note: Both pledge a herd girl to the man who, unafraid of the black bull's fury, takes it (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான்); in the Kalittokai her kin give her to the catcher, in the epic no bull is penned.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the bull-catch pledge word for word but drops the contest, so a herders' marriage custom survives as the names of dance roles in a rite against ill omen.

gains.a: the pledge gains its origin in a real contest in which a girl's kin give her to the man who takes the bull
gains.b: the custom gains a later life, recited over girls as a ritual formula with no bull and no catcher

links.note: In the idyll the old women seek an omen and hear a herd girl tell a distressed tethered calf that its mothers will soon come; in the epic the herd's own signs foretell sorrow and the herdswoman dances so that the cows' and calves' distress may pass.
links.teaches: Both read a calf's distress among the herds as a sign about an absent man, but the idyll's chance word promises a return and the epic's signs announce a death the herders do not yet know, so the mullai omen-scene is turned from hope to loss.

gains.a: the rite gains its convention: in mullai poetry an omen among the herds speaks of an absent husband, which lets the signs point at Kovalan without naming him
gains.b: the idyll's comforting omen gains a counterpart in which the same kind of sign foretells a husband's death and a rite fails to turn it

links.note: The first signs, milk that will not set and a weeping bull, come on the morning after Kovalan has been cut down at the king's word.
links.teaches: Read after the killing, the omens are no forecast but the herd registering a death its keepers have not heard of, so the reader holds the meaning the characters lack.

links.note: The herders' omens fall in the cowshed (the cattle's bells drop, the cows tremble); the queen's fall in the court (the falling umbrella and sceptre, the trembling gate bell).
links.teaches: The same wrong is signalled first in the house of the victim's hosts and later in the king's own house, each through the things of its own life, so the omens move from the cowshed to the throne as the consequence nears the king.

links.note: The kuravai is danced so that the coming distress may pass; at the dance's end an uproar from the town brings the news of Kovalan's death.
links.teaches: The rite meant to turn the sorrow away becomes the frame in which the sorrow arrives, so the herders' remedy is shown powerless against a deed already done.

links.note: Aiyai and her mother likened Kannaki to the one of their clan who relieved the gem-coloured god's distress in the Yamuna; here the girl cast as Pinnai garlands the girl cast as Mayavan while Kannaki looks on.
links.teaches: Because the herdswomen had already seen Kannaki as Pinnai and Kovalan as the dark god, the dance's Pinnai garlanding Mayavan plays out before Kannaki the union that has, unknown to her, already ended.

new_concepts.gloss: the herders' round dance with linked hands, danced by the girls and the young men after the bull-catch
new_concepts.label_source: Used in Silappathikaram 17 as குரவை (lines 25, 61); id as used in the Kalittokai marks

new_concepts.gloss: the herders' bull-catch: young men leap at fighting bulls in the pen, and a herd girl is promised to the man who takes a bull
new_concepts.label_source: id as used in the Kalittokai marks; Silappathikaram 17 lines 27 to 43 give its pledges (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான், அடர்த்தாற் குரிய, தொழுவிடை ஏறு குறித்து வளர்த்தார்)

new_concepts.gloss: an omen read from the body or from creatures (sneezing, a throbbing eye, a lizard's chirp, an owl's cry) as a sign of the absent lover's thought or return
new_concepts.label_source: the Tholkappiyam's term for omens, id as used in the Kainnilai marks; Silappathikaram 17 lines 11 to 20 give the signs in the herd (வருவதோர் துன்பமுண்டு)

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: id as used in the Valayapathi marks; Silappathikaram 17 lines 48 to 49 and 72 to 74 name the seven notes (குரல் துத்தம் கைக்கிளை உழை இளி விளரி தாரம்)

source_issues: Line 13 reads உருகா உருகும் where the prose restatement (lines 18 to 19) has உருகாமையும்; the couplet's sense is unsure.
Line 18 was repaired by the build (a doubled vowel sign reduced to one).

Lines 31 to 32 and 37 to 38 pledge girls to the rider of a young bull in nearly the same words, as do lines 33 to 34 and 35 to 36 for the spotted white bull; the text may carry a doubling, though seven bulls are needed for seven girls.
Line 58 (முத்தைக்கு நல்விளரி தான்) is obscure, and vilari is placed twice (lines 56 and 58).
